genesis 1 1
The Torah opens with its first word, Bereshit, "in the beginning." Everything that follows starts here: the world has a Maker, and it did not come about by chance.
genesis 1 3
The first thing God makes is light, and He makes it with words. In Judaism speech has real power, so the words we choose each day matter.
genesis 1 27
Every person is made in the image of God. That is why each human life has worth, whoever the person is and wherever they come from.
genesis 1 31
After each day God saw that it was good. On the sixth day, with people in the world, it became "very good." Look for the good in your own day.
genesis 2 3
This is the first Shabbat. God rested on the seventh day and made it holy, and we rest on it too. Shabbat is a gift of time, not only a rule.
genesis 2 15
Adam was put in the garden to work it and to guard it. The earth is placed in our care, and looking after it is part of our job.
genesis 2 18
"It is not good to be alone." People need each other. Community, friendship and family are part of how we were made.
genesis 4 9
Cain asks, "Am I my brother's keeper?" The rest of the Torah answers yes. We are responsible for one another.
genesis 12 1
Lech lecha: "go for yourself." Abraham leaves everything familiar to follow God. Every new start, including learning Hebrew, takes a first step like this.
genesis 12 2
Abraham is told not only that he will be blessed but that he will be a blessing. A good life is one that brings good to others.
genesis 15 5
God takes Abraham outside to count the stars. When things feel small or uncertain, step back and look at the bigger picture.
genesis 18 25
Abraham argues with God to save the people of Sodom. In Jewish tradition it is right to speak up for justice, even before the highest authority.
genesis 28 15
Jacob is alone and running away, and God promises: I am with you, wherever you go. You are never as alone as you feel.
genesis 28 16
Jacob wakes from his dream and says God was in this place and he did not know it. Holiness can be right where you are, if you notice it.
genesis 32 11
Before meeting his brother Esau, Jacob says he is not worthy of all the kindness he has received. Gratitude and humility go together.
genesis 45 4
Joseph says to the brothers who sold him, "Come close to me." It is one of the great moments of forgiveness in the Torah.
genesis 50 20
Joseph tells his brothers that what they meant for harm, God turned to good. Hard chapters of a life can lead somewhere good.
exodus 3 5
At the burning bush Moses is told to take off his shoes, because the ground is holy. Some moments call for us to slow down and pay attention.
exodus 3 14
Ehyeh asher ehyeh: "I will be what I will be." God's name here is about being present, in every time and place.
exodus 13 8
This verse is why we tell the Passover story at the Seder. Each generation tells it as if it happened to them.
exodus 14 14
At the Sea of Reeds, Moses tells the frightened people that God will fight for them. Sometimes the right move is to stay calm and trust.
exodus 15 2
From the Song at the Sea: "The Lord is my strength and my song." These words are sung in synagogue every morning.
exodus 15 11
Mi chamocha, "Who is like You?" This line from the Song at the Sea is part of the daily prayers, just after the Shema.
exodus 19 6
At Sinai the whole people is called a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Holiness is meant for everyone, not only for a few.
exodus 20 2
The Ten Commandments begin with who God is: the One who brought us out of slavery. Freedom comes first, and the commandments follow.
exodus 20 8
Zachor: "Remember the Shabbat day." We remember it with candles, Kiddush, rest and time with the people we love.
exodus 20 12
Honour your father and your mother. It is one of the Ten Commandments, and the first that comes with a promise of long life.
exodus 22 20
Do not wrong the stranger, because you were strangers in Egypt. This idea comes up again and again in the Torah.
exodus 23 2
Do not follow the crowd to do wrong. Doing the right thing sometimes means standing apart.
exodus 23 9
"You know the heart of the stranger." Our own history should make us kind to newcomers.
exodus 25 8
"Make Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them." Not "in it," but among them: God lives among people, in the places they make holy.
exodus 33 13
Moses asks God, "Show me Your ways, so that I may know You." Learning is one of the ways Jews come close to God.
exodus 34 6
These are God's qualities of mercy, sung on the High Holy Days: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, full of kindness and truth.
leviticus 19 2
"You shall be holy, for I am holy." The chapter that follows shows what that means: honesty, kindness and fairness in everyday life.
leviticus 19 3
Respect your parents and keep Shabbat. Both are about honouring where we come from.
leviticus 19 9
Leave the corners of your field for people in need. Giving to others is built right into how we earn and spend.
leviticus 19 14
Do not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind. Treat everyone with care, especially those who cannot defend themselves.
leviticus 19 16
Do not spread gossip, and do not stand by while your neighbour is in danger. Words can hurt, and silence can too.
leviticus 19 18
"Love your neighbour as yourself." Rabbi Akiva called this the great principle of the whole Torah.
leviticus 19 32
Rise before the elderly and honour them. Age brings wisdom, and the Torah asks us to show it respect.
leviticus 25 10
"Proclaim liberty throughout the land." These words about the Jubilee year are cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.
numbers 6 24
The first line of the Priestly Blessing, still said in synagogues and by parents to children on Friday night.
numbers 6 26
The Priestly Blessing ends with shalom, peace. In Hebrew, shalom also means wholeness: everything in its right place.
numbers 11 29
When others begin to prophesy, Moses is not jealous. He wishes everyone could share God's spirit. Great leaders lift others up.
numbers 15 39
This verse is about the tzitzit, the fringes on the tallit. Seeing them is a reminder of the commandments and of who we want to be.
numbers 24 5
Mah tovu, "How good are your tents." Many synagogues open the morning service with these words.
deuteronomy 4 9
Do not forget what you have seen, and teach it to your children and grandchildren. Memory is how a people stays alive.
deuteronomy 6 4
The Shema, the central line of Jewish prayer: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One." It is said morning and night.
deuteronomy 6 5
V'ahavta: love God with all your heart, all your soul and all your strength. Faith in Judaism is about love, not only belief.
deuteronomy 6 7
Talk about these words at home, on the road, when you lie down and when you get up. That is why the Shema is said at bedtime and in the morning.
deuteronomy 8 3
"A person does not live by bread alone." We need meaning, learning and purpose as much as food.
deuteronomy 8 10
Eat, be satisfied, and bless. This verse is the source of Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after meals.
deuteronomy 10 19
Love the stranger, because you were strangers in Egypt. The Torah asks for more than not hurting newcomers; it asks us to love them.
deuteronomy 16 20
Tzedek tzedek tirdof: "Justice, justice you shall pursue." The word is said twice, to show how hard we should work for it.
deuteronomy 30 14
The Torah is not far away: it is in your mouth and in your heart. It is within reach, one word at a time.
deuteronomy 30 19
"Choose life." Every day brings choices, and the Torah asks us to choose the ones that lead to life and blessing.
deuteronomy 31 6
Chazak ve'ematz: "Be strong and of good courage." Moses says this before the people enter the land without him.
deuteronomy 6 6
"These words shall be upon your heart." Learning Torah is meant to go deeper than memory, into who we are.
exodus 31 16
V'shamru: the people of Israel shall keep the Shabbat for all generations. This verse is sung on Friday night and Shabbat morning.
deuteronomy 34 10
Near the very end of the Torah: no prophet arose like Moses, who knew God face to face. Then we roll the scroll back and start again.
